book: 140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See

chapters.relation: Aaron Ehasz, ATLA's head writer, reflects that the show tested its characters' belief systems against their humanity: Aang's attempt to comfort himself with Buddhist detachment fails when Appa is taken, and he cannot let go of his love for Katara to unblock his final chakra and enter the Avatar State. Yet Uncle Iroh shows the opposite lesson, since by studying Water Tribe ideas he invents lightning redirection, the technique that lets Zuko survive his father and lets Team Avatar save the world. The preface concludes that philosophy both limits and unlocks human potential, capped with a joke about Hegel and hard ice cream.

De Cruz and De Smedt argue that ATLA subverts the Chosen One trope: Aang's training is slow and non-linear, he needs dedicated teachers, and saving the world is a team effort in which Katara leads and Sokka plans. The show's central theme is oneness, voiced by Guru Pathik's 'illusion of separation' ('The Guru') and Huu's banyan-grove tree ('The Swamp'), which the editors trace to Daoist, Huayan Buddhist (Fazang's golden lion), and Indigenous traditions of interdependence. They frame the volume's engagement with genocide, imperialism, ecological destruction, and Ba Sing Se's authoritarian denial as proof that philosophy is needed for human flourishing.

chapters.file: ch09 - PART I THE UNIVERSE OF AVATAR.md

chapters.relation: Belarde-Lewis (Zuni/Tlingit) and Bordeaux (Lakota) read ATLA through Indigenous philosophy: V.F. Cordova's 'bounded space' explains how each nation's landscape shapes its people and benders, with Tui and La, the badgermoles, flying bison, and dragons as other-than-human teachers, and Shawn Wilson's relationality frames Yue's sacrifice, the Lion Turtle's elder wisdom, and the Order of the White Lotus as intergenerational balance rather than power. Aang's energybending of Ozai ('Sozin's Comet') shows that balance across generations matters more than power over the world, and the Lion Turtle makes the universe '(Lion) Turtles all the way down'.

Ortiz-Hinojosa asks what is most fundamental in ATLA's world, testing Toph's metalbending, lava- and sandbending, energybending, and the Spirit World against Empedocles' four roots, Anaximander's undifferentiated apeiron, Heraclitus's fire and flux, the Nahua teotl, and Chinese qi and Hindu prana. She concludes that energy is plausibly the fundamental basis from which the four Elements differentiate, making the deepest reality of ATLA a non-physical interdependence, while stressing that even Guru Pathik and the past Avatars lack complete knowledge of their own universe, just as we do.

Isrow maps each bending art to its real martial art and source philosophy: Katara's Taiji waterbending embodies Daoist wu-wei when she forgoes revenge on Yon Rha ('The Southern Raiders'); Toph's Hong Jia earthbending expresses the Buddhist eightfold path's Right Speech through her insistence on truth; Zuko's Northern Shaolin firebending enacts the Four Noble Truths, his desire-driven suffering ending only when he abandons chasing the Avatar; and Aang's Daoist Baguazhang airbending makes freedom openness to change, shown in his receptivity to Iroh's advice. The Avatar's true power is combining these character strengths, not merely wielding four elements.

Whittaker argues ATLA is an abolitionist text about nationhood itself: the show first naturalizes the four nations through the four elements, so that Hama and Zuko are expelled from their host communities the moment their bending is revealed ('The Puppetmaster', 'Zuko Alone'), much as Beauvoir showed gender is naturalized from sex. It then denaturalizes both through Huu's swamp unity, Iroh bending fire like water ('Bitter Work'), and Guru Pathik's 'illusion of separation'. Drawing on Black abolitionism and Denise Ferreira da Silva's 'difference without separability', he concludes Aang's task is not to save a world of nations but to make the world like him.

chapters.file: ch14 - A Specter Is Haunting the Bending World.md
chapters.relation: Lin argues the Bending World's supernatural inequality breaks Hobbes's condition that even the weakest can kill the strongest, the equality that motivates the social contract, so might-is-right is magnified: Ozai rules without bargaining while weak Earth Kings become Dai Li figureheads. Energybending's built-in 'moral self-destruct' needs no earthly accountability, resembling the divine right of kings rather than Arendt's insight that violence eradicates politics, and Aang wisely remains a passive guardian. The Avatar's reincarnation creates recurring power vacuums, and because bending is a non-redistributable endowment, the Equalist revolution haunts the Bending World like the specter of communism in the Communist Manifesto.

chapters.file: ch16 - Spirituality Similar Ways of Seeing the World.md
chapters.relation: Cloud, an Ojibwe author, compares ATLA's worldview with Anishinaabe teachings: the Water Tribe's depiction (Sokka's war paint and Great Lakes-style club in 'The Avatar Returns') gave him, as a ten-year-old, the first media reflection of his own identity against the 'vanishing Indian' myth. Hei Bai's rage over the scorched forest and the koi spirits Tui and La match Basil Johnston's manidoog, spirits 'just as much a reality as trees', while Huu's one-tree swamp ('The Swamp') embodies the dreamcatcher's single strand that connects all beings, and the unresolved mysteries of the swamp teach respectful comfort with the unknowable.

Wawrzyniak traces Sokka's growth from seeing animals as food and fur ('Dinner!' at Momo in 'The Southern Air Temple') to bonding with Foo Foo Cuddlypoops and vowing a 'karmically correct vegetarian existence', measured against Kant's anthropocentric view of animals as mere things whose cruel treatment matters only as a risk to human morals. Aang's harm-free uses of animals, from otter penguin sledding to riding hog monkeys, are then tested by Korsgaard's pathocentrism: animals are 'someones' who mind what happens to them, so even harmless use demands justification. The chapter urges us to scrutinize our own habits of eating, entertainment, and pet-keeping with Sokka-style empathy.

Flowers argues bloodbending is morally neutral: like Huu's plantbending ('The Swamp') and taijiquan's qinna joint locks, it is an advanced technique whose harm depends on the practitioner's intention, as Katara's gentle suppression of Hama ('The Puppetmaster') shows against her vengeful contortion of the Southern Raider. Waterbending's Taiji foundation, with the yin-yang harmony of Tui and La's circling koi and the Aikido/Aikijutsu contrast in applying kotegaeshi, grounds his conclusion from Yagyu Munenori's Heiho Kadensho: Hama practiced the sword that takes life, while Katara's compassionate bloodbending is 'bending that saves life'.

chapters.file: ch19 - What if Hama Was Wrong.md
chapters.relation: Gregory argues bloodbending necessarily uses persons as mere means because it overrides the victim's will regardless of their actual consent, unlike buying tea from Zuko but like Azula's deception of Long Feng, and so violates Kant's Formula of Humanity in every offensive use. Katara's bloodbending of Hama in self-defense is permissible because she stops Hama's wrong rather than using her toward any end, and even a hypothetical consensual 'cooperative model' cannot redeem the practice, since the sheer power it grants and its corrupting effects on practitioners (Noatak and Tarrlok in LoK) justify Katara's ban.

Wilhelm uses expected utility theory to defend the villagers of 'The Fortuneteller': given their complete confidence in Aunt Wu's prediction that they will meet their true love wearing red shoes, wearing red shoes every day maximizes expected value, so Sokka's charge of irrationality fails. A formal appendix with credence and valuation functions proves the red-shoes strategy rational and generalizes to the villager who stays calm during the platypus bear attack, concluding that mystical and empirical reasoning do not differ in kind: both can be rational or irrational.

Fice reads ATLA through the feminist ethics of care, using Joan Tronto's phases of caring-about, taking care of, and care-giving to analyze Katara: freeing Aang from the iceberg, offering to heal Zuko's scar in the Crystal Catacombs, and her full arc as the Painted Lady feeding, healing, and freeing a polluted village. Care also misfires ('Imprisoned') and is devalued as feminine 'women's work' when Toph calls Katara motherly ('The Runaway'), a myth the chapter rejects. Care scales politically too: the Gaang's defeat of Fire Nation imperialism is care repairing the world, while Azula's indifference to Ty Lee and Mai marks her villainy.

chapters.file: ch22 - “I knew I’d know it when I knew it” (King Bumi, “Sozin's Comet, Part 2 The Old Masters”).md
chapters.relation: Skirry and Skirry read the Gaang's journey as building 'ethical-epistemological maps' in the manner of Native American and Inuit Traditional Knowledge (pijitsirniq, respect for land and community), against the Fire Nation's epistemology of control that pollutes rivers and brainwashes schoolchildren ('The Headband'). Where Descartes' lone meditator says 'I think, therefore I am' and uses dreams to cast doubt on experience, the Gaang's Native-style epistemology holds 'We think, therefore I am': Aang's prophetic dreams ('The Avatar and the Fire Lord'), his vision of Toph ('The Swamp'), spirit-world journeys, and the counsel of past Avatars and the Lion Turtle are genuine knowledge that resolves his dilemma about killing Ozai.

chapters.file: ch24 - Avatar The Reunion of Multiplicity.md
chapters.relation: Strok explains the swamp visions in 'The Swamp' (Katara's dead mother, Sokka's Yue, Aang's glimpse of the girl who will be Toph) through Plotinus's teaching that time is 'the life of the Soul' and Augustine's three presents of memory, attention, and expectation, so that past and future are present to the soul and Huu's 'time is an illusion and so is death' becomes literal metaphysics. The banyan-grove tree, one organism spread over miles, models Neoplatonic emanation from the One, and this unity explains the Avatar's communion with past and future selves as well as Aang's refusal to kill Ozai, since death, like time, is a misperception.

Kellen builds successive definitions of lying through ATLA cases: Aang's 'Bonzu Pippinpaddleopsicopolis' alias, non-linguistic disguises versus Toph's 'I'm blind!' mere misleading, brainwashed Jet whose false statements are not lies ('Lake Laogai'), and Azula's battleship metaphor ('The Beach'), arriving at Carson's warranting contexts to count the Dai Li's 'There is no war in Ba Sing Se' and Azula's '400-foot-tall purple platypus bear' as Sorensen's bald-faced lies told without intent to deceive. Frankfurt's bullshit explains Aunt Wu's fortunetelling, and the conclusion is political: bald-faced lies corrode the trust on which communities rest, so we must refuse to live in a real-world Ba Sing Se.

holes.name: Fazang
holes.what: Tang-dynasty Huayan Buddhist patriarch who illustrated the oneness of reality to Empress Wu Zetian through the metaphor of a golden lion statue.
holes.why: Chapter 8's account of ATLA's central theme of oneness is built on Fazang's 'Essay on the Golden Lion' and its claim that all things lack individual nature.

holes.name: The Chosen One Trope
holes.what: The fantasy narrative convention in which a pre-destined savior with innate powers, rather than collective struggle and learning, saves the world.
holes.why: Chapter 8's first argument is that ATLA subverts this trope: Aang's slow training, need for teachers, and dependence on Team Avatar replace passive salvation by an innate hero.

holes.name: V. F. Cordova
holes.what: Jicarilla Apache philosopher whose Native American metaphysics centers 'bounded space', the land base that shapes and obligates the people formed by it.
holes.why: Chapter 10's entire reading of the four nations, their benders, and their landscapes is organized around Cordova's concept of bounded space.

holes.name: Indigenous Relationality
holes.what: The Indigenous ontological thesis that persons, land, animals, spirits, and ancestors are bound in relations of mutual responsibility and accountability to a specific place.
holes.why: Chapter 10 argues ATLA's bending, spirit world, Lion Turtle lore, and Order of the White Lotus express relationality and elder knowledge rather than Western power metaphysics.

holes.name: Empedocles
holes.what: Presocratic who held that four ungenerated roots (Earth, Water, Air, Fire) are mixed and separated by the forces Love and Strife.
holes.why: Chapter 11 uses Empedocles' four roots as the closest ancient analogue to ATLA's four bendable Elements and its question of whether they are fundamentally distinct.

holes.name: Anaximander
holes.what: Presocratic who posited the apeiron, an unlimited undifferentiated origin from which the opposites generate and to which they return.
holes.why: Chapter 11 models ATLA's energy as Anaximander's apeiron, the single fundamental substance from which the four Elements might be generated.

holes.name: Teotl (Nahua metaphysics)
holes.what: The Aztec (Nahua) doctrine that everything is fundamentally teotl, a single divine energy in constant motion and becoming.
holes.why: Chapter 11 compares the Sun Warriors' fire-as-life-energy to James Maffie's account of teotl to test whether ATLA's reality is one dynamic substance.

holes.name: Qi (vital energy)
holes.what: The Chinese concept of a vital energy or life force flowing through bodies and the world, cultivated in practices like qigong.
holes.why: Chapter 11 identifies ATLA's bending energy and Guru Pathik's chakras with qi (and Hindu prana) to argue energy underlies the four Elements.

holes.name: Abolitionism (prison and institution abolition)
holes.what: A theory of justice, built from Black radical thought, holding that unjust institutions are not buggy but essentially unjust and so must be abolished rather than reformed.
holes.why: Chapter 13 argues ATLA itself offers an abolitionist account: the four nations, like prisons for prison abolitionists, are a rotten arrangement that must be abolished, not saved.

holes.name: Denise Ferreira da Silva
holes.what: Contemporary theorist who critiques the modern 'grammar' of separability, determinacy, and sequentiality and proposes 'difference without separability'.
holes.why: Chapter 13 takes its central thesis, that the elements' and nations' differences need not ground separation, from her Black abolitionist critique of modern racializing thought.

holes.name: Anishinaabe Worldview (manidoog and interconnectedness)
holes.what: The Ojibwe/Anishinaabe way of seeing in which manidoog (spirits) are as real as trees and valleys, creation is one interconnected whole, and the ultimate ground is mystery.
holes.why: Chapter 16 reads ATLA's Water Tribe, Hei Bai, Tui and La, and the swamp's single living tree through Anishinaabe teachings the author received from his elders.

holes.name: Yagyu Munenori
holes.what: Seventeenth-century Japanese sword master whose Heiho Kadensho teaches the distinction between the sword that takes life and the sword that gives life.
holes.why: Chapter 18's conclusion that bloodbending is morally neutral and intention-dependent rests on Munenori's katsujinken/satsujinken distinction.

holes.name: Katsujinken (the life-giving sword)
holes.what: The martial-ethical ideal of using technique to suppress an opponent with minimal harm (the life-giving sword) rather than to dominate or kill (the life-taking sword).
holes.why: Chapter 18 applies this exact distinction to bloodbending: Hama's use takes life while Katara's restrained, compassionate use saves life.

holes.name: Expected Utility Theory
holes.what: The standard philosophical theory of rational decision-making: an agent is rationally required to act when the expected value of acting exceeds that of not acting.
holes.why: Chapter 20 uses expected utility theory (with a formal appendix) to prove that the villagers' red-shoes faith in Aunt Wu is rational, refuting Sokka's empiricism.

holes.name: Joan Tronto
holes.what: Political philosopher who defines care as a species activity that maintains and repairs our world and distinguishes its phases: caring about, taking care of, and care-giving.
holes.why: Chapter 21 structures its entire analysis of Katara and the Gaang's politics around Tronto's definition and phases of care.

holes.name: Native American Epistemology (ethical-epistemological maps)
holes.what: Indigenous approaches to knowledge that tie knowing to ethical attentiveness, community, place, ritual, dreams, and visions rather than individualist control.
holes.why: Chapter 22 reads the Gaang's growth as building evolving ethical-epistemological maps in this tradition, against the Fire Nation's epistemology of control.

holes.name: Roy Sorensen
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher who introduced 'bald-faced lies', undisguised lies told without any intention to deceive the audience.
holes.why: Chapter 25's central puzzle, the Dai Li's 'There is no war in Ba Sing Se', is analyzed as precisely Sorensen's bald-faced lies.
